items.stem: Which conclusion can best be drawn from this excerpt?

options.1: Europeans understood and respected Native American cultural traditions.
options.2: Religious freedom was guaranteed in Pennsylvania.
options.3: Native Americans had great respect for the king of England.

items.rationale: Gachradodow explicitly contrasts two legal orders ('You have your Laws and Customs, so have we') inside a treaty council — the act of talking across difference is the answer. (1) inverts the speaker's complaint. (2) imports Pennsylvania's founding myth the text never mentions. (3) is contradicted by 'God did not approve of it.'

options.1: Native Americans were allowed to maintain control of their ancestral lands.
options.2: American expansion continued to push Native Americans west.
options.3: Native Americans remained neutral during the American Revolution.

items.rationale: Outcome question, not a comprehension question. (1) and (4) are wish-fulfillment distractors — they tempt because the document is sympathetic. (3) is factually false (Brant, Oneida). Students who read tone instead of outcome pick (1).

items.stem: The events described in this account could be considered a turning point in history because

options.1: The author of this account went on to become a powerful English Lord.
options.2: Native American societies grew strong again after contracting European diseases, resulting in an increase in Native populations at this time.
options.3: Native Americans in the British colonies experienced a drastic decline in population due to disease and war brought by Europeans.
options.4: New England colonists repaired relationships with Native Americans soon after the incidents described.

items.citation: Source: John Josselyn, An Account of Two Voyages to New-England, Made during the Years 1638, 1663
items.rationale: Correct=(3). The passage names plague then smallpox, three populous Massachusetts kingdoms cut from 30,000 to 300, and the Pequots destroyed by the English. (2) inverts it. (1) is nowhere in the account. (4) is contradicted by the same sentence that names the destruction.
hints: A 'turning point' needs a big, lasting shift — what changed permanently for the people described?
Look at the population numbers Josselyn gives — from 30,000 down to 300.

items.stem: Based on the information provided in this account, which claim is most plausible?

options.1: Native American peoples were welcoming to European colonists who settled in North America.
options.2: Native American populations were susceptible to diseases to which they had no previous exposure.
options.3: European colonists poisoned Native peoples intentionally, decimating their population.
options.4: Native American civilization was far inferior to European civilization.

items.citation: Source: John Josselyn, An Account of Two Voyages to New-England, Made during the Years 1638, 1663
items.rationale: Correct=(2). The mortality struck 'not long before the English came' and again by smallpox when they did — no previous exposure. (3) asserts deliberate poisoning the account never states, and is the distractor that punishes reading intent into a source. (1) is not addressed. (4) is a value judgment, not a claim the source supports.
hints: What does the account say happened right around when the English arrived — and again later?
'Not long before the English came' and then smallpox afterward — that's exposure, not intent.

items.stem: Which claim is best supported by both documents?

options.1: Colonial political institutions were not influenced by English legal traditions.
options.2: Colonial political institutions failed to represent the interests of colonial inhabitants.
options.3: Colonial political institutions were influenced by both English legal tradition and colonial experience.
options.4: Colonial political institutions guaranteed suffrage for all adults who lived in the colonies.

citation: Source: Emily Arendt et al., “Colonial Society” in The American Yawp, Stanford University Press, 2018
items.rationale: Correct=(3). Doc 1 supplies the English legal tradition — consent to taxation through a representative great council; Doc 2 supplies the colonial experience — wider white male suffrage and more local power. The word 'both' is doing the work. (1) is refuted by Doc 1's presence in the pair. (2) Doc 2 says colonial government had MORE popular involvement. (4) 'all adults' overreaches: Doc 2 says white male suffrage.
hints: The word 'both' matters here — what does each document contribute separately?
One document gives you English legal tradition; the other gives you what changed once colonists were on their own.

items.stem: According to these documents, a key difference between political institutions in England and its colonies centered around

options.1: the scope and variety of powers held by their representative bodies
options.2: the age at which a man was entitled to vote in elections
options.3: who had the authority to raise taxes from the people
options.4: The percentage by which a law could be passed in their representative bodies

citation: Source: Emily Arendt et al., “Colonial Society” in The American Yawp, Stanford University Press, 2018
items.rationale: Correct=(1). Doc 2: colonial assemblies 'regulated businesses, imposed new taxes, cared for the poor, built roads and bridges, and made most decisions concerning education' — 'more power in a variety of areas'. That phrase is the answer nearly verbatim. (3) is the strong trap and the reason this item is worth BK's eye: both documents locate the taxing power in a representative body, so taxation is a SIMILARITY, not the difference. (2) and (4) are not discussed in either document.
items.needs_bk: Distractor (3) is a defensible reading if BK intended taxation as the difference. As written, the textual echo points at (1).
hints: Careful — both documents actually agree on who could raise taxes, so that's not the difference.
Look at what colonial assemblies are doing beyond taxes — roads, schools, businesses. Compare that range to England's.
